recorded_justifications.note: Montgomery and Vaughan prove the unsubtracted identity, with the constant left implicit and the sum over zeroes taken in the symmetric order. THIS NODE STATES THE DIFFERENCE OF THAT IDENTITY AT TWO POINTS, and the step from theirs to this is subtraction: nothing analytic is added and nothing is weakened. What subtraction buys is that the constant cancels -- so no normalisation has to be pinned down -- and that the terms become (w-s)/((s-rho)(w-rho)) = O(1/|rho|^2), hence absolutely summable, so the claim can be made with HasSum and carries its own convergence. THE SUBTRACTED FORM IS ALSO THE FORM CONSUMERS USE. Titchmarsh Theorem 9.6(A), and its explicit version as Chirre-Helfgott's prop:titch96A, evaluate the identity at s and at s_+ = sigma_+ + i t with sigma_+ > 1 and subtract; the unsubtracted version never appears. Davenport chapter 12 gives the same identity, as does Titchmarsh's own chapter 3. IMPORTS `none`, AND IT IS A REAL NONE. s and w are universally quantified with every side condition a hypothesis, so this conclusion consumes nothing from the network. A LEAN SOLUTION IS NOT CHEAP. It would need the Hadamard factorisation of xi -- order-one entire function, Jensen's formula, the product over zeroes -- none of which Mathlib has. That is why the designated justification is the literature and not a receipt; see `limitations`.

The obvious choice -- the complement of the integers, open by isClosed_range_intCast -- is too small for the statement as made here, because the hypotheses admit even integers s >= 2 (at s = 2 every side condition holds, cos(pi) = -1 included). The solution uses {z | 1 < z.re} union (range Int.cast)^c instead: a union of two opens, on each of which the functional equation applies, and which contains s in both cases -- if s is not an integer the second piece has it, and if it is, the hypotheses force it past 2.
